analysis.investment_thesis: ABLBL is a newly incorporated (2024) apparel retailer carrying premium brand portfolio (Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Reebok) but priced at 73x trailing P/E and 48x EV/EBITDA, implying an earnings yield of roughly 1.4% — far below the Magic Formula's 12% threshold. Despite an adequate ROCE of 25%, the combination of sky-high leverage (D/E 2.67), a razor-thin operating margin (8.88%), and near-zero earnings yield makes this an unattractive Magic Formula candidate.
key_strengths: Established lifestyle brand portfolio (LP, Van Heusen, Allen Solly) with pricing power in premium apparel
ROCE of 25.45% suggests the underlying brands generate decent returns on tangible capital
Reasonable FII/DII ownership (16%/17%) signals institutional interest despite newness
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~1.4% (P/E 73x) is severely overvalued by Magic Formula standards — no margin of safety
High financial leverage (D/E 2.67) depresses ROE to just 9.78% despite decent ROCE, meaning debt is destroying shareholder value
Company incorporated in 2024 — zero multi-year earnings track record to validate ROIC sustainability
red_flags: EV/EBITDA of 48x: implies earnings would need to grow dramatically for years just to justify current price
ROE (9.78%) materially below ROCE (25.45%) — high-cost debt is consuming most of the business's economic returns
No historical income statement or balance sheet data available — cannot verify ROIC durability
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula requires two things simultaneously: a cheap price (earnings yield >12%) and a good business (ROIC >20%). ABLBL fails the first test decisively. With EBIT/EV implied around 1.4% and EV/EBITDA at 48x, the market is pricing in years of flawless execution — and paying for it upfront. The only redeeming factor is ROCE at 25.45%, which confirms the brand asset base does earn above-average returns, but that figure is almost certainly inflated by the newness of the balance sheet post-carve-out.

The 2.67x debt-to-equity ratio is a serious concern: interest costs are eating into the gap between ROCE and ROE, leaving shareholders with just 9.78% return. For a Magic Formula investor, the ideal is a business that earns high ROIC AND is available cheap — ABLBL offers neither. Until the P/E compresses below 20x and we have at least 3 years of verified ROIC track record, this is a pass.
